title: Bryan Station Siege, August 1782
summary: In August 1782 British officers and several hundred allied warriors besieged Bryan Station on Elkhorn Creek near Lexington — a camp from 1775–76 that settlers fortified in 1779.
bodyMarkdown:
Bryan Station, also written Bryan's or Bryant's, sat on the south bank of Elkhorn Creek a few miles northeast of [Lexington](/stories/lexington-named/). The [state marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/bryans-station) says the brothers Morgan, James, William, and Joseph Bryan camped there in 1775–76. They came from North Carolina and were kin by marriage to [Daniel Boone](/people/#daniel-boone). In 1779 the camp was fortified as a station.

By the summer of 1782 the Revolution was winding down in the East, but not in the West. From Detroit, British officers kept sending raids south with their Native allies. In August, [Capt. William Caldwell](/people/#william-caldwell) of Butler's Rangers and the interpreter [Simon Girty](/people/#simon-girty) led a force of rangers with several hundred Wyandot, Lenape, and Shawnee warriors toward the Kentucky settlements.

On August 15–16 they surrounded Bryan Station. The attackers hoped to draw the men out, and to catch the garrison at the spring outside the walls. The fort was short of water, and the spring sat just outside the stockade.

The defenders guessed the plan. They sent the women and girls out with their usual pails, as on any morning, so the hidden warriors would think the fort suspected nothing. An [ExploreKYHistory account](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/592) of the siege notes that two Kentuckians also slipped out and reached Lexington to call for help. The women filled the fort's supply and walked back up the hill unharmed.

The fight that followed did not take the station. Caldwell's force burned crops, killed livestock, and pulled back north.

Kentucky militia gathered quickly to chase them. Three days later, on August 19, they caught up at the Licking River crossing and rode into an ambush at [Blue Licks](/stories/battle-of-blue-licks/). It was one of the worst defeats of the frontier war. [Simon Girty's story at Bryan Station](/stories/simon-girty-interpreter-at-bryan-station-1782/) and [Hugh McGary's](/stories/hugh-mcgary-the-blue-licks-hothead/) carry the rest of the story.

## Kentucky today

State historical marker #21, "Bryan's Station," stands on Bryan Station Road (KY 57) in northeast Fayette County. Near it, the Lexington Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution dedicated a stone memorial wall at the spring in August 1896, in honor of the women of Bryan Station. The spring and fort site are on private land and not open to the public.
